content.text:
Humans have lit the coast for as long as they have gone to sea, and the lighthouse is the most durable form of that effort. The most famous early example was the Pharos of Alexandria, built on the island of Pharos at the entrance to the harbour in the third century BC, probably during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus. Its builder was Sostratus of Cnidus, and the ancient writer Lucian preserved an inscription that claimed the tower was raised by Sostratus "to the gods who save, on behalf of sailors." Estimates of its height range widely, but it was likely well over one hundred metres, rising in stages of stone with a fire at the top. It was admired as one of the wonders of the ancient world, and its name survives in the modern word for lighthouse in several languages, including the Greek *pharos* and the Italian *faro*. The Pharos was damaged by earthquakes over the centuries and had collapsed by the fourteenth century, its stones reused in later fortifications.

The Romans built lighthouses along their maritime routes, and some survive. The Tower of Hercules at A Coruña in north-western Spain, a stone structure around fifty metres tall, dates from the Roman period and is still in service, which makes it the oldest lighthouse still operating. Roman towers at Dover and at several Mediterranean ports show that the technique was widespread, and that the state or municipal authorities paid for lights in the same way they paid for roads and harbour walls. Like the Pharos, these towers burned wood or coal in open hearths at the top, and their light was a matter of sheer fuel and altitude. The fire needed constant tending, and the tower had to be high enough that the glow could be seen over the horizon.

After the fall of Rome, the record grows thinner, but the need did not disappear. Many medieval lights were kept by religious houses, which had both the resources and the motive to guide pilgrims and merchants. Some were simple beacons on headlands or church towers, and others were maintained by fishing communities. In the Middle Ages, lights were often private enterprises, supported by tolls levied on ships passing a harbour or headland. This pattern of private ownership, funded by dues rather than general taxation, persisted in parts of Europe for centuries. In England, the Corporation of Trinity House received a royal charter from Henry VIII in 1514 to manage pilotage and to erect and maintain aids to navigation. Trinity House would remain responsible for lights around England and Wales for the next five hundred years, and its history illustrates how the lighthouse straddled public duty and commercial interest.

The problem that defined the early modern lighthouse was the open sea rock. A tower on a shoal or a reef could save many ships, but building one was dangerous, expensive, and often impossible with the materials and engineering of the day. The Eddystone Rock, about fourteen miles off Plymouth in England, was a notorious hazard. In 1698 Henry Winstanley, a wealthy eccentric who was also a gifted designer of ornamental fountains, built a wooden lighthouse on the rock. It was elaborate, decorated, and visibly fragile. Winstanley himself, who liked to test his work in storms, is said to have remarked that he wished to be in it during the worst gale that could blow. He got his wish in 1703, when a great storm destroyed the tower, and he was lost with it along with the keepers.

The second Eddystone lighthouse, designed by John Rudyerd and built of timber, lasted until 1755, when it was destroyed by fire. The engineer who replaced it, John Smeaton, changed the science of the subject. Smeaton studied the properties of mortar and found that a lime mortar mixed with clay would set under water, which was crucial for construction on a tidal rock. He designed the tower so that its granite blocks were dovetailed together, each course locked to the one beneath, so that the whole formed a single mass that waves could not easily tear apart. Smeaton's tower was completed in 1759 and stood for well over a century. When the rock beneath it was found to be eroding, the tower was dismantled in the 1880s and re-erected on Plymouth Hoe, where it still stands as a monument. Smeaton's principles of stone construction and hydraulic lime influenced engineers far beyond Britain, and his tower became a model for later rock lighthouses.

Other rock lights followed in the same spirit. The Bell Rock off the coast of Angus in Scotland was a vicious reef submerged at high tide, and the Northern Lighthouse Board commissioned Robert Stevenson to build a light there. Construction began in 1807 and the light was first shown in 1810. The work required the building of a temporary house on the rock, where the workers lived during the short windows of calm weather, and it was carried out with great discipline. Stevenson's family would become the dominant name in Scottish lighthouse engineering. His sons and grandsons, including Alan, David, and Thomas Stevenson, built dozens of lights around the coasts of Scotland and beyond, and Thomas's son Robert Louis Stevenson, the novelist, grew up with the family trade and wrote about it with affection. Their work at places like Skerryvore, a remote rock in the Hebrides completed in 1844, showed how much engineering could be done with patience, precise stone cutting, and careful planning of landings and supplies.

The most important single advance in lighthouse optics came from France. In the late eighteenth century, the Argand lamp, with its hollow circular wick and glass chimney, had made lighthouse lamps much brighter, but a flame still radiated light in every direction, and most of it was wasted. Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a French physicist working on the wave theory of light, devised a lens made of concentric glass prisms and rings that could gather light from a lamp and bend it into a horizontal beam. Fresnel's lenses were built in ranks or orders, the largest of which could throw a beam visible for many miles. The first of his lenses was installed at the Cordouan light at the mouth of the Gironde in 1823, and within a few decades they had been adopted throughout Europe and across the world. The lenses were expensive and delicate, but they transformed the range of a light. A lighthouse that once threw a dim glow could now project a beam tens of kilometres out to sea, and the rotating mechanisms, driven by clockwork weights or floating in a bath of mercury, gave each light a distinctive pattern so that sailors could identify it.

The lighthouse also developed a human side that is part of its mythology. Keepers lived on station for long periods, often in isolated places, and their work required them to trim wicks, polish lenses, wind clockwork, and keep logs. Families sometimes lived with them, and the rhythm of daily life on a rock or a remote headland was shaped by the light. The keepers were also, at times, rescuers. The best-known example in English-speaking countries is Grace Darling, daughter of the keeper of the Longstone light in the Farne Islands. In 1838, during a storm, she and her father rowed out to the wreck of the steamship *Forfarshire* and rescued survivors, and her story became a national sensation. Keepers in many countries performed similar rescues, and lighthouse service was often regarded as a vocation that combined technical skill with personal courage.

The United States developed its lighthouse system in the same period, though its early history was more fragmented. Boston Light, first lit in 1716 on Little Brewster Island in Boston Harbor, was the first lighthouse in the American colonies, and it was destroyed by British forces during the Revolutionary War before being rebuilt. In 1789 the new federal government passed a Lighthouse Act that placed the aids to navigation under the Treasury Department, a decision that gave the nation a central responsibility for the coasts. Over the next century the service grew in size and technical sophistication, and in 1852 a Lighthouse Board was established to oversee the work. The Lighthouse Service was eventually transferred to the Department of Commerce and then, in 1939, to the Coast Guard, which continued to manage the lights through the twentieth century.

Across the twentieth century, the technology of the lighthouse changed more rapidly than at any time since the Fresnel lens. Oil lamps gave way to incandescent electric bulbs, and then to more powerful sources. Radio beacons, radar, and fog signals of various kinds supplemented the visual light, and the sound of a foghorn or a diaphone became as characteristic of the coast as the beam itself. Automation steadily reduced the number of people required to tend a station. Light sensors switched lamps on at dusk, motors rotated lenses without human help, and remote monitoring allowed a single center to supervise many lights at once. Many countries withdrew their keepers from lights that had once required a full crew. The United States automated its manned lights over the latter part of the century, and by its end very few remained staffed.

Satellite navigation has now made the lighthouse less central to the safety of shipping than it once was. Ships carry electronic charts that show their position to within metres, and they receive warnings of hazards by radio and digital systems. Lighthouses remain in service, however, because they are cheap to run, reliable, and independent of electronic failure. Modern lights use LED lamps powered by solar panels and batteries, and many are fitted with radio transmitters that can be checked from afar. Some have been converted into museums, holiday rentals, or heritage sites, and many are protected as historic structures. The Pharos of Alexandria is gone and its stones have been scattered for centuries, but the basic purpose it served remains: a fixed point of light on a dangerous coast, kept burning so that those at sea can find the way home.
